intro.heading: The folder looks complete. Is it?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A manager and her deputy are tidying the policy folder before a busy quarter. Every policy is there, and a few have coloured tabs from past reviews. Then the deputy reads the infection control policy properly. It still carries wording from the pandemic. The safeguarding policy names a body that no longer exists under that name. The medication policy has a gap where a name should go. Nobody did anything wrong. The documents were fine once, and time moved on. The manager now needs a list, not a hunch. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The home reviews its policies. Tabs go on the folder.
New staff are told to read the folder. Most do.
The manager is confident the set is in good order.
Pandemic era wording stays in the infection control policy.
An old agency name sits in the safeguarding policy.
A placeholder such as [insert name] was never filled in.
Three policies have no review date recorded anywhere.
“When was this last reviewed, and what changed?” The manager has tabs, not answers.

trail_close: The policies were never the problem. The gap is between a folder that looks current and one you can prove is. Here is how CareStream gives you the list, using your own documents.

items.q: How does CareStream tell me which policies are out of date?
items.a: You upload your policies, then run the Scan policies step on the Gaps page. It checks the text for superseded names, pandemic era wording, unfilled placeholders, thin content and overdue review dates, and gives each policy a severity and a score. It is a fixed check with no AI in it, so you get the same list each time for the same text.

items.q: Does it find every outdated point?
items.a: No. It finds what its catalogue of signals knows about. It does not read for clinical accuracy and it cannot tell whether your own procedure is wise. Treat it as a fast first pass that you follow with your own review.

items.q: What happens when it finds something?
items.a: You open Review and fix. For superseded terms it pre fills the old wording with the current term from the catalogue, so you can check it and accept it. Nothing is changed for you without you looking, and you can ignore a finding for one policy or for the whole account.

items.q: What about policies with no review date?
items.a: They are counted, not marked as faults. You then set a date and an interval, such as 6 months, 12 months, 2 years or 3 years, and that policy joins your review schedule. Once a date is past, it appears in the Policies due for review panel and you get one reminder email per review cycle.

items.q: Can I tell staff when a policy changes?
items.a: Yes, in the sense that you can allocate an adhoc training module on that topic, built from your own policies where they cover it. Staff complete it in the Staff Hub, and a wrong answer becomes a short lesson. Changing a policy does not trigger training by itself. You choose to allocate it.

items.q: Does it keep a record of policy versions?
items.a: Document version history is on every plan. Uploading a replacement raises the version number and the older one is kept in History. CareStream records that staff read a policy, with time and whether they pressed Mark as read. It does not record signatures or which version a read was against.

There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to see the scan on up to 5 of your own policies. The pricing page shows what each plan includes.

limits.heading: A plain list of what to look at, not a verdict

cards.title: It does not find every outdated point
cards.body: The scan matches known signals such as old names, pandemic wording and blanks. It cannot judge clinical accuracy or spot every change in practice.

cards.title: It does not rewrite policies on its own
cards.body: Fixes are suggestions you check and accept. Wording from the gap checks is drafted by our own machine learning and is for you to review, adapt and approve.

cards.title: It is not legal advice or a guarantee
cards.body: A clean scan does not guarantee compliance or a CQC rating. Full scanning of a large library, gap fixes and approvals are on Professional and above.

items.q: What counts as outdated policies in the scan?
items.a: Old names for bodies, laws and frameworks, pandemic era wording, unfilled placeholders such as XXXX, TBC or [insert name], very little content or no purpose or scope, and overdue or missing review dates. Each finding is high, medium or low.

No. The out of date scan is a fixed check and uses none of your AI tokens. Some other gap checks, such as example wording, are drafted by our own machine learning and are suggestions for you to review.

items.q: Can I run a policy update check on only a few policies?
items.a: Yes. The free plan screens up to 5 uploaded policies in total. Upload your most used policies first, such as infection control, safeguarding and medication.

items.q: Does it replace my own review?
items.a: No. It gives you a starting list so your review is quicker. You still decide what is right for your service. See how often care policies should be reviewed.

items.q: How do I set up a policy review schedule?
items.a: Record a last reviewed date and an interval for each policy: 6 months, 12 months, 2 years or 3 years. Overdue policies show in the Policies due for review panel, and the admins get a reminder email.

items.q: What is a good policy review checklist?
items.a: Start with the checklist in the guide below: names, dates, placeholders, who it applies to, and who needs to know about any change. The scan covers the first few for you.

items.q: Does CareStream do policy version control?
items.a: Document version history is on every plan, and a replacement upload raises the version number while the older one stays in History. Edited policies approved on Professional and above get major version numbers. See care policy version control.

items.q: Which care home policies should I scan first?
items.a: Start with the ones staff use daily or that carry the most risk, such as safeguarding, medication and infection prevention and control, then work through the rest of your care home policies.

guide.heading: A practical way to run a policy review
guide.lede: A review does not need a weekend. It needs a short list of what to check, a date, and a record of what changed. Regulation 17 on good governance asks for systems or processes that are established and operated effectively, and that let you assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the service. The regulation does not name policies, but a dated review is one simple way to show that you do this.

sections.h3: Why staff training follows the policy
paragraphs: A policy that changes is only useful once the people doing the work know about it. Regulation 18 on staffing says employed persons must receive such appropriate support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal as is necessary to carry out their duties. After any policy update, a short check on the change shows whether staff took it in.

sections.h3: A policy review checklist you can copy
checklist: Names: do bodies, laws and frameworks still carry their current names?
Blanks: are there placeholders, such as a missing role or a TBC?
Dates: is there a last reviewed date and a next review date on record?
People: who needs to hear about the change, and have they been checked on it?

sections.h3: Set a rhythm and keep the record
paragraphs: Pick an interval that suits each policy, put it on record, and let the reminder do the nagging. Keep the old version in your history and note what changed. Then the answer to “when was this last reviewed?” takes seconds, not an afternoon.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the scan result, the review date, the version history and the staff check together, so you can show what you found and what you did about it.
